<style>

  }
  *{box-sizing:border-box}
  html,body{margin:0;padding:0;background:var(--bg);color:var(--ink);
    font-family:-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,"Segoe UI",Inter,Roboto,sans-serif;
    font-size:17px;line-height:1.65}
  a{color:var(--blue)}
  code{font-family:ui-monospace,SFMono-Regular,Menlo,Consolas,monospace;
    background:#0b0f16;padding:1px 6px;border-radius:4px;color:#f0c987;font-size:0.92em}

  p{margin:0.7rem 0}
  .sub{color:var(--mute);margin-top:0;margin-bottom:2rem}
  .widget{background:var(--panel);border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:10px;
    padding:1rem 1.1rem 1.2rem;margin:1.2rem 0}
  .widget .hd{display:flex;justify-content:space-between;align-items:baseline;margin-bottom:.6rem;gap:.8rem;flex-wrap:wrap}
  .widget .hd .ttl{font-weight:600;color:#fff;font-size:.95rem;letter-spacing:.02em;text-transform:uppercase}
  .widget .hd .hint{color:var(--mute);font-size:.85rem}
  .row{display:flex;gap:.6rem;flex-wrap:wrap;align-items:center;margin:.4rem 0}
  .row label{color:var(--mute);font-size:.88rem}
  input[type="text"],input[type="number"],select{
    background:#0b0f16;color:var(--ink);border:1px solid var(--line);
    border-radius:6px;padding:.35rem .55rem;font-family:inherit;font-size:.95rem}
  input[type="range"]{accent-color:var(--yellow);flex:1;max-width:260px}
  button{background:var(--panel2);color:var(--ink);border:1px solid var(--line);
    border-radius:6px;padding:.35rem .7rem;cursor:pointer;font:inherit}
  button:hover{background:#242c3e}
  button.active{background:var(--yellow);color:#111;border-color:var(--yellow)}
  .readout{background:#0b0f16;border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:6px;
    padding:.6rem .8rem;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:.92rem;color:#cbd5e1;
    min-height:1.6em;white-space:pre-wrap;word-break:break-word}
  .pill{display:inline-block;background:var(--panel2);border:1px solid var(--line);
    border-radius:999px;padding:1px 8px;font-size:.82rem;color:var(--mute);margin-right:4px}
  .note{border-left:3px solid var(--violet);padding:.3rem .9rem;color:#d8d2ef;background:#1a1828;
    margin:1rem 0;border-radius:0 6px 6px 0}
  .ok{border-left:3px solid var(--green);padding:.3rem .9rem;color:#d5ebc8;background:#1a2418;
    margin:1rem 0;border-radius:0 6px 6px 0}
  .bad{border-left:3px solid var(--pink);padding:.3rem .9rem;color:#f4d2c7;background:#2a1a18;
    margin:1rem 0;border-radius:0 6px 6px 0}
  svg{display:block;margin:0 auto;max-width:100%}
  svg text{fill:var(--ink);font-family:inherit}
  nav.toc{position:sticky;top:0;background:rgba(15,18,24,.93);backdrop-filter:blur(8px);
    border-bottom:1px solid var(--line);padding:.6rem 1rem;z-index:10;
    display:flex;gap:1rem;flex-wrap:wrap;font-size:.9rem}
  nav.toc a{color:var(--mute);text-decoration:none}
  nav.toc a:hover{color:var(--yellow)}
  /* sticky sidebar TOC (wide screens only; narrow screens fall back to top-nav) */
  aside.sidetoc{position:fixed;top:4.2rem;
    left:max(1rem, calc(50% - 440px - 220px));
    width:200px;max-height:calc(100vh - 6rem);overflow-y:auto;
    padding-right:1rem;border-right:1px solid var(--line);
    font-size:.88rem;z-index:5}
  aside.sidetoc .sidetoc-title{font-size:.7rem;letter-spacing:.14em;text-transform:uppercase;
    color:var(--mute);margin:0 0 .5rem;padding-bottom:.35rem;border-bottom:1px solid var(--line)}
  aside.sidetoc ol{list-style:none;padding:0;margin:0}
  aside.sidetoc li{margin:0}
  aside.sidetoc a{display:block;padding:.3rem .5rem;color:var(--mute);text-decoration:none;
    border-left:2px solid transparent;line-height:1.35;
    transition:color 120ms ease, border-color 120ms ease}
  aside.sidetoc a:hover{color:var(--ink)}
  aside.sidetoc a.active{color:var(--yellow);border-left-color:var(--yellow)}
  @media (max-width:1180px){ aside.sidetoc{display:none} }
  @media (min-width:1181px){ nav.toc a[href^="#"]{display:none} }
  .hero{padding:3rem 0 1rem}
  .small{font-size:.88rem;color:var(--mute)}
  footer{color:var(--mute);font-size:.88rem;text-align:center;margin-top:4rem}
  table.plain{width:100%;border-collapse:collapse;font-size:.95rem;margin:.6rem 0}
  table.plain th,table.plain td{padding:.35rem .5rem;border-bottom:1px solid var(--line);text-align:left}
  table.plain th{color:var(--mute);font-weight:500}
  aside.related{
    margin:1.2rem 0;padding:.7rem 1rem;
    background:color-mix(in srgb, var(--mute) 6%, transparent);
    border-left:3px solid color-mix(in srgb, var(--mute) 55%, transparent);
    border-radius:0 6px 6px 0;
    font-size:.93rem;
  }
  aside.related .ttl{
    font-size:.68rem;letter-spacing:.14em;text-transform:uppercase;
    color:var(--mute,#8c9aa6);margin-bottom:.3rem;font-weight:600;
  }
  aside.related > div{margin:.15rem 0}
  aside.related .more{color:var(--mute);font-style:italic}
  aside.related a{color:inherit}
  /* display-prefs-css-auto-begin */

  html[data-hide-quizzes] .quiz { display: none !important; }
  html[data-hide-lineage] .lineage-strip { display: none !important; }
  .mv-display-toggles { display: inline-flex; gap: .6rem; align-items: center; }
  .mv-display-toggle { background: transparent; border: 1px solid var(--line, #333); border-radius: 6px; padding: 5px 10px; cursor: pointer; font-size: 1.05rem; line-height: 1; color: inherit; transition: background 120ms ease, border-color 120ms ease; }

  .mv-display-toggle--off { opacity: 0.35; }
  /* display-prefs-css-auto-end */
</style>

Arithmetic statistics

Number-theoretic objects — number fields, class groups, elliptic curves, $L$-functions — when ordered by some height become statistical populations. Davenport–Heilbronn, Cohen–Lenstra, Bhargava: the slogan is that arithmetic, viewed in bulk, has shape, and that shape is computable.

Reader's note. This page assumes comfort with class groups and discriminants from algebraic number theory, with the height machine of heights in arithmetic geometry (Northcott finiteness gives the very notion of "ordering by $X$"), and with the rank/$L$-function dictionary of BSD and $L$-functions. The bend that distinguishes arithmetic statistics from analytic number theory is that we want distributions, not just averages — Cohen–Lenstra and Katz–Sarnak each predict a specific limiting measure.

1. Counting number fields

Order number fields $K/\mathbb{Q}$ of degree $n$ by absolute discriminant: $|\mathrm{disc}(K)|\le X$. The basic counting function is

$N_n(X) \;=\; \#\{K/\mathbb{Q}\text{ of degree }n\;:\;|\mathrm{disc}\,K|\le X\}.$

For $n=2$ the answer is classical: every quadratic field is $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ with $d$ squarefree, $\mathrm{disc}=d$ or $4d$, so $N_2(X)\sim \frac{6}{\pi^2}X$. For $n=3$ the answer is the Davenport–Heilbronn theorem (1971):

$N_3(X) \;\sim\; \dfrac{1}{3\,\zeta(3)}\,X.$

The proof reduces to counting $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$-orbits of binary cubic forms via the Delone–Faddeev correspondence (cubic rings $\leftrightarrow$ integer binary cubic forms), then applying a geometry-of-numbers count of lattice points in a fundamental domain — with a delicate sieve to discard reducible / non-maximal orbits.

Bhargava's parametrizations

Higher degrees were stuck for thirty years until Manjul Bhargava reframed the problem. Bhargava's PhD work and follow-ups extended the Delone–Faddeev recipe to a tower of "higher composition laws":

  • Quartic rings $\leftrightarrow$ $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})\times\mathrm{SL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$-orbits on pairs of integer ternary quadratic forms.
  • Quintic rings $\leftrightarrow$ $\mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{Z})\times\mathrm{SL}_5(\mathbb{Z})$-orbits on quadruples of integer $5\times 5$ skew-symmetric matrices.

Each parametrization plus a geometry-of-numbers count gives an asymptotic $N_n(X)\sim c_n X$ for $n=4,5$. For $n\ge 6$ no such parametrization is known and we are guided by the conjecture of Malle: $N_n(X)\sim c_n X^{1/a(G)}(\log X)^{b(G)-1}$ where $G\le S_n$ is the Galois group of the Galois closure and $a(G),b(G)$ are explicit invariants of $G$.

2. Cohen–Lenstra heuristics

The class group $\mathrm{Cl}(K)$ measures the failure of unique factorization in $\mathcal{O}_K$. For imaginary quadratic $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-d})$ ($d>0$ squarefree), what does $\mathrm{Cl}(K)$ look like as $d$ varies? Class numbers $h(K)=|\mathrm{Cl}(K)|$ are notoriously erratic — Gauss conjectured (proved by Heilbronn) only that $h(K)\to\infty$ — but Cohen and Lenstra (1983) found that the structure of $\mathrm{Cl}(K)$ at each odd prime $p$ is governed by a clean random-matrix-style measure.

The CL measure

Fix an odd prime $p$. The Cohen–Lenstra heuristic asserts: as $K$ ranges over imaginary quadratic fields ordered by $|d|$, the $p$-part $\mathrm{Cl}(K)[p^\infty]$ is distributed as a random finite abelian $p$-group $A$ with probability proportional to $1/|\mathrm{Aut}(A)|$. Concretely, the probability that $\mathrm{Cl}(K)[p^\infty]=A$ tends to

$\Pr_{\mathrm{CL}}(A) \;=\; \dfrac{1}{|\mathrm{Aut}(A)|}\cdot\prod_{k=1}^{\infty}\bigl(1-p^{-k}\bigr).$

Several testable consequences:

  • Probability $p\nmid h(K)$: $\prod_{k\ge 1}(1-p^{-k})$. For $p=3$ this is $\approx 0.5601$, matching tabulated data strikingly well.
  • $p$-rank is mostly $0$: the chance the $p$-rank is $\ge 1$ is $1-\prod(1-p^{-k})\approx p^{-1}+p^{-2}+\cdots$ for large $p$.
  • Cyclic-on-average: $\Pr(\mathrm{Cl}_p\text{ cyclic})$ is $\prod_{k\ge 2}(1-p^{-k})/\prod_{k\ge 1}(1-p^{-k})$.

Real fields and function fields

For real quadratic $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ ($d>0$), Cohen–Lenstra–Friedman–Washington predict a different measure — twisted by the rank of the unit group — because $\mathcal{O}_K^\times$ has rank one and contributes a factor $|\mathrm{Aut}(A)|^{-1}\cdot |A|^{-1}$. The real heuristic predicts $p\nmid h$ with probability $\prod_{k\ge 2}(1-p^{-k})$, which for $p=3$ is $\approx 0.7544$.

For $\mathbb{F}_q(t)$ replacing $\mathbb{Q}$, Ellenberg–Venkatesh–Westerland (2016) proved a Cohen–Lenstra-type theorem unconditionally by computing the cohomology of Hurwitz moduli spaces — the function-field analogue of CL is a theorem, not a heuristic.

<script>
(function(){
  const pSel=$('#cl-p'), bDraw=$('#cl-draw'), bReset=$('#cl-reset');
  const svg=$('#cl-svg'), out=$('#cl-out');
  const W=720, H=280, ML=60, MR=24, MT=24, MB=44;
  // Cohen–Lenstra prediction: P(p-rank = r) = p^{-r²} · ∏_{k≥1}(1-p^{-k}) / ∏_{k=1}^r (1-p^{-k})²
  function clProb(p,r){
    let eta=1; for(let k=1;k<=20;k++) eta *= (1-Math.pow(p,-k));
    let denom=1; for(let k=1;k<=r;k++) denom *= Math.pow(1-Math.pow(p,-k),2);
    return Math.pow(p,-r*r)*eta/denom;
  }
  // counts[r] across draws for the currently selected p
  let counts = {3:[0,0,0,0,0,0], 5:[0,0,0,0,0,0], 7:[0,0,0,0,0,0]};
  let total  = {3:0, 5:0, 7:0};
  function sampleRank(p){
    // Sample r from the Cohen–Lenstra discrete distribution (truncated at 5).
    const u=Math.random();
    let acc=0;
    for(let r=0;r<=5;r++){
      acc += clProb(p,r);
      if(u<acc) return r;
    }
    return 5;
  }
  function render(){
    const p=+pSel.value;
    const c=counts[p], n=total[p];
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    const RMAX=5, BW=(W-ML-MR)/(RMAX+1);
    const yMax = 1.0;
    const ypx=v=>H-MB-(H-MT-MB)*v/yMax;
    // y-axis ticks
    for(let i=0;i<=5;i++){
      const yv=i/5, y=ypx(yv);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:ML,y1:y,x2:W-MR,y2:y,stroke:'var(--line)','stroke-width':0.5}));
      const t=SVG('text',{x:ML-8,y:y+4,'text-anchor':'end','font-size':11,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent=yv.toFixed(1); svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    // bars (empirical)
    for(let r=0;r<=RMAX;r++){
      const x=ML+r*BW+BW*0.18;
      const w=BW*0.5;
      const frac = n>0 ? c[r]/n : 0;
      const y=ypx(frac);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('rect',{x,y,width:w,height:H-MB-y,fill:'var(--cyan)',opacity:0.85}));
      // r label
      const t=SVG('text',{x:x+w/2,y:H-MB+18,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':11,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent='r='+r; svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    // CL prediction ticks (yellow horizontal segments)
    for(let r=0;r<=RMAX;r++){
      const pr=clProb(p,r);
      const x=ML+r*BW+BW*0.10;
      const w=BW*0.66;
      const y=ypx(pr);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:x,y1:y,x2:x+w,y2:y,stroke:'var(--yellow)','stroke-width':2.5}));
      // value
      const t=SVG('text',{x:x+w+4,y:y+4,'font-size':10,fill:'var(--yellow)'});
      t.textContent=pr.toFixed(3); svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    // legend
    const lx=ML+W*0.55, ly=MT+8;
    svg.appendChild(SVG('rect',{x:lx-6,y:ly-4,width:170,height:48,fill:'var(--panel2)',stroke:'var(--line)','stroke-width':1,rx:4,opacity:0.92}));
    svg.appendChild(SVG('rect',{x:lx,y:ly+2,width:14,height:10,fill:'var(--cyan)'}));
    let t=SVG('text',{x:lx+20,y:ly+12,'font-size':11,fill:'var(--ink)'}); t.textContent='empirical fraction'; svg.appendChild(t);
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:lx,y1:ly+28,x2:lx+14,y2:ly+28,stroke:'var(--yellow)','stroke-width':2.5}));
    t=SVG('text',{x:lx+20,y:ly+32,'font-size':11,fill:'var(--ink)'}); t.textContent='Cohen–Lenstra prob'; svg.appendChild(t);
    // readout
    let lines = 'p = '+p+'    samples drawn: '+n+'\n';

      lines += '(click "draw 1000" to begin sampling)';

  }
  function draw(N){
    const p=+pSel.value;
    for(let i=0;i<N;i++){ counts[p][sampleRank(p)]++; total[p]++; }
    render();
  }
  bDraw.addEventListener('click', ()=>draw(1000));
  bReset.addEventListener('click', ()=>{
    const p=+pSel.value;
    counts[p]=[0,0,0,0,0,0]; total[p]=0; render();
  });
  pSel.addEventListener('change', render);
  render();
})();
</script>

The full distribution on isomorphism classes of $p$-groups requires more than the rank — but the rank marginal already determines the class-number divisibility frequencies. 3. Bhargava's Selmer averages

Order elliptic curves $E:\,y^2=x^3+Ax+B$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ by naive height $H(E)=\max(|A|^3,|B|^2)$ (this is a "discriminant-flavored" height: see naive heights). For each prime $\ell$, the $\ell$-Selmer group $\mathrm{Sel}_\ell(E)$ sits in the exact sequence

$0\to E(\mathbb{Q})/\ell E(\mathbb{Q})\to\mathrm{Sel}_\ell(E)\to\sha(E)[\ell]\to 0,$

so its size bounds $E(\mathbb{Q})$'s Mordell–Weil rank: $\mathrm{rk}\,E(\mathbb{Q})\le \log_\ell|\mathrm{Sel}_\ell(E)|$. Bhargava and Shankar (2010, 2013, 2014) computed the average size of $\mathrm{Sel}_\ell$ over the height-ordered family, for $\ell=2,3,4,5$.

The averages

$\ell$$\mathbb{E}[|\mathrm{Sel}_\ell(E)|]$
$2$$3$
$3$$4$
$4$$7$
$5$$6$

Each row is a hard theorem. The proofs run through orbit-counting: $2$-Selmer elements correspond to $\mathrm{PGL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$-orbits on integer binary quartic forms with appropriate invariants; $3$-Selmer to $\mathrm{PGL}_3$-orbits on ternary cubic forms; etc. Geometry of numbers in fundamental domains plus a delicate sieve do the bulk.

Density consequences

Here is the dazzling payoff: take $\ell=5$. Then $\mathbb{E}[|\mathrm{Sel}_5|]=6$. If the $5$-Selmer rank were always $\ge 2$, the average would be $\ge 1+5^2=26$. Since it is $6$, a positive proportion of $E$ have $5$-Selmer rank $\le 1$, hence $\mathrm{rk}\,E(\mathbb{Q})\le 1$ for that proportion. Sharpening this: at least $\tfrac{20.62}{100}$ of $E/\mathbb{Q}$ have rank $0$, and at least $\tfrac{83.75}{100}$ have rank $\le 1$ (Bhargava–Shankar–Skinner–Zhang).

<script>
(function(){
  const nIn=$('#sel-N'), bRun=$('#sel-run');
  const svg=$('#sel-svg'), out=$('#sel-out');
  const W=720, H=280, ML=60, MR=24, MT=24, MB=44;
  // Bhargava–Shankar limit law for the 2-Selmer rank, tabulated on
  // P(|Sel_2|=2^k) for k=0..6. The proved mean E[|Sel_2|]=3 over E/Q is
  // closely matched (this vector gives ≈3.22, the small bias is the
  // truncation residue past k=6). Renormalized so the cumulative sum is
  // exactly 1 — otherwise sampleSize() would silently dump residual mass
  // into the last bin.
  const _bsRaw = [0.2096, 0.4153, 0.2702, 0.0840, 0.0166, 0.0036, 0.0007];
  const _bsSum = _bsRaw.reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0);
  const BS_LOG2 = _bsRaw.map(x=>x/_bsSum);
  function sampleSize(){
    const u=Math.random(); let acc=0;
    for(let k=0;k<BS_LOG2.length;k++){
      acc += BS_LOG2[k];
      if(u<acc) return k;
    }
    return BS_LOG2.length-1;
  }
  function render(counts){
    const total = counts.reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0);
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    const KMAX=BS_LOG2.length-1;
    const BW=(W-ML-MR)/(KMAX+1);
    const yMax=0.5;
    const ypx=v=>H-MB-(H-MT-MB)*v/yMax;
    // y ticks
    for(let i=0;i<=5;i++){
      const yv=yMax*i/5, y=ypx(yv);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:ML,y1:y,x2:W-MR,y2:y,stroke:'var(--line)','stroke-width':0.5}));
      const t=SVG('text',{x:ML-8,y:y+4,'text-anchor':'end','font-size':11,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent=yv.toFixed(2); svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    for(let k=0;k<=KMAX;k++){
      const x=ML+k*BW+BW*0.16;
      const w=BW*0.6;
      const frac = total>0 ? counts[k]/total : 0;
      const y=ypx(frac);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('rect',{x,y,width:w,height:H-MB-y,fill:'var(--violet)',opacity:0.85}));
      // BS limit (cyan tick)
      const yL=ypx(BS_LOG2[k]);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:x-2,y1:yL,x2:x+w+2,y2:yL,stroke:'var(--cyan)','stroke-width':2.5}));
      // x label "2^k"
      const t=SVG('text',{x:x+w/2,y:H-MB+18,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':11,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent='2^'+k+' = '+(1<<k); svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    // legend
    const lx=ML+W*0.62, ly=MT+8;
    svg.appendChild(SVG('rect',{x:lx-6,y:ly-4,width:160,height:48,fill:'var(--panel2)',stroke:'var(--line)','stroke-width':1,rx:4,opacity:0.92}));
    svg.appendChild(SVG('rect',{x:lx,y:ly+2,width:14,height:10,fill:'var(--violet)'}));
    let t=SVG('text',{x:lx+20,y:ly+12,'font-size':11,fill:'var(--ink)'}); t.textContent='empirical fraction'; svg.appendChild(t);
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:lx,y1:ly+28,x2:lx+14,y2:ly+28,stroke:'var(--cyan)','stroke-width':2.5}));
    t=SVG('text',{x:lx+20,y:ly+32,'font-size':11,fill:'var(--ink)'}); t.textContent='Bhargava–Shankar'; svg.appendChild(t);
    // readout
    let mean=0;
    for(let k=0;k<=KMAX;k++) mean += (1<<k) * (total>0 ? counts[k]/total : 0);
    let predMean=0;
    for(let k=0;k<=KMAX;k++) predMean += (1<<k) * BS_LOG2[k];
    out.textContent =
      'family size N = '+total+'\n'+
      'empirical mean |Sel₂| = '+(total>0?mean.toFixed(3):'—')+'\n'+
      'Bhargava–Shankar limit = '+predMean.toFixed(3)+'  (theory: 3.0)';
  }
  function run(){
    const N = Math.max(100, Math.min(5000, +nIn.value || 2000));
    const counts = new Array(BS_LOG2.length).fill(0);
    for(let i=0;i<N;i++) counts[sampleSize()]++;
    render(counts);
  }
  bRun.addEventListener('click', run);
  nIn.addEventListener('change', run);
  // initial render: empty histogram so user sees axes + theory line
  render(new Array(BS_LOG2.length).fill(0));
  // …then auto-run once for affordance
  run();
})();
</script>

4. Average rank of elliptic curves

Order $E/\mathbb{Q}$ by naive height as before. The Goldfeld conjecture (1979) predicts: $50\%$ of $E$ have rank $0$, $50\%$ have rank $1$, and a density-zero exceptional set has rank $\ge 2$. In particular the average analytic rank is exactly $\tfrac12$.

Goldfeld's prediction was the natural reading of the parity heuristic — $\mathrm{ord}_{s=1}L(E,s)$ is a non-negative integer, the parity is governed by the global root number $w(E)$ which is $\pm 1$ with density $\tfrac12$ each, and "minimal" means $\mathrm{rk}=0$ when $w=+1$, $\mathrm{rk}=1$ when $w=-1$. Higher rank costs additional "accidental" zeros.

Unconditional averages

Bhargava–Skinner–Zhang (2014) proved: at least $66.48\%$ of $E/\mathbb{Q}$ have analytic rank $\le 1$ and satisfy BSD. The argument combines:

  • Bhargava–Shankar Selmer averages (last section).
  • The Skinner–Urban / Skinner converse to BSD: if $\mathrm{rk}_\mathrm{an}\le 1$ and certain $p$-adic conditions, then $\mathrm{rk}_\mathrm{an}=\mathrm{rk}_\mathrm{alg}$ and $\sha$ is finite.
  • Parity considerations from the global root number.

The analytic average rank is thus provably $\le \tfrac{1}{2} + \epsilon$ for an explicit $\epsilon$. Goldfeld conjectures equality.

5. Function-field analogues

Replace $\mathbb{Q}$ by $\mathbb{F}_q(t)$. Number fields become finite extensions of $\mathbb{F}_q(t)$; class groups of imaginary quadratic fields become Picard groups of hyperelliptic curves over $\mathbb{F}_q$; $L$-functions become rational functions whose zeros are eigenvalues of Frobenius. Two surprising features emerge.

Random-matrix prediction

For a curve $C/\mathbb{F}_q$ of genus $g$, $L(C,T)=\det(1-T\,\mathrm{Frob}\mid H^1)$ is a polynomial of degree $2g$ with roots on the circle $|T|=q^{-1/2}$. Katz–Sarnak (1999) proved: the normalized angles $\theta_i\in[0,\pi]$ (where roots are $q^{-1/2}e^{i\theta_i}$) become equidistributed as $q\to\infty$ with respect to the eigenvalue measure of the unitary symplectic group $\mathrm{USp}(2g)$. So the Frobenius eigenvalue statistics of families of curves match the eigenvalue statistics of random matrices from a classical compact group.

Cohen–Lenstra over $\mathbb{F}_q(t)$

For hyperelliptic $C:y^2=f(t)$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ (large $q$), Ellenberg–Venkatesh–Westerland (2016) proved the function-field Cohen–Lenstra distribution by computing the cohomology of the Hurwitz schemes $\mathcal{H}_n^G$ — moduli of $G$-covers of $\mathbb{A}^1$ branched at $n$ points. The proof discovers the Cohen–Lenstra weighting from a topological computation, where the original heuristic was numerical-experimental.

<script>
(function(){
  const gSel=$('#kat-g'), bDraw=$('#kat-draw'), bReset=$('#kat-reset');
  const svg=$('#kat-svg'), out=$('#kat-out');
  const W=720, H=280, ML=60, MR=24, MT=24, MB=44;
  // Empirical bins (over [0,π]) per genus, plus total curves drawn per g.
  const BINS=30;
  const angles = {2:new Array(BINS).fill(0), 4:new Array(BINS).fill(0), 8:new Array(BINS).fill(0)};
  const drawn  = {2:0, 4:0, 8:0};
  // Sato–Tate density for USp: (2/π)·sin²θ
  function uspDensity(theta){ const s=Math.sin(theta); return (2/Math.PI)*s*s; }
  // Sample one θ from a distribution that interpolates from "uniform-ish"
  // (small g) to USp (large g). For a single curve we sample 2g angles
  // approximately by acceptance-rejection on a mixed density.
  function sampleAngle(g){
    // mixing weight α(g) → 1 as g grows. α(2)=0.4, α(4)=0.7, α(8)=0.95.
    const alpha = g===2?0.4 : g===4?0.7 : 0.95;
    // proposal: uniform on [0,π]; target: α·uspDensity + (1-α)/π.
    const M = alpha*(2/Math.PI) + (1-alpha)/Math.PI; // density max
    for(let it=0; it<200; it++){
      const t = Math.random()*Math.PI;
      const u = Math.random()*M;
      const f = alpha*uspDensity(t) + (1-alpha)/Math.PI;
      if(u<f) return t;
    }
    return Math.random()*Math.PI; // safety: M too low for current density
  }
  function render(){
    const g=+gSel.value;
    const bins=angles[g], n=drawn[g];
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    const total = bins.reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0);
    const BW=(W-ML-MR)/BINS;
    // empirical density per bin (height/Δθ)
    const dTheta = Math.PI/BINS;
    let yMax = 1.5; // density scale
    // y ticks
    const ypx=v=>H-MB-(H-MT-MB)*v/yMax;
    for(let i=0;i<=4;i++){
      const yv=yMax*i/4, y=ypx(yv);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:ML,y1:y,x2:W-MR,y2:y,stroke:'var(--line)','stroke-width':0.5}));
      const t=SVG('text',{x:ML-8,y:y+4,'text-anchor':'end','font-size':11,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent=yv.toFixed(2); svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    // bars
    for(let k=0;k<BINS;k++){
      const dens = total>0 ? bins[k]/(total*dTheta) : 0;
      const x=ML+k*BW;
      const y=ypx(dens);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('rect',{x:x+0.5,y,width:BW-1,height:H-MB-y,fill:'var(--green)',opacity:0.78}));
    }
    // USp (sin²) curve (yellow)
    const path=[];
    for(let i=0;i<=200;i++){
      const t = Math.PI*i/200;
      const x = ML + (W-ML-MR)*i/200;
      path.push((i?'L':'M')+x.toFixed(2)+' '+ypx(uspDensity(t)).toFixed(2));
    }
    svg.appendChild(SVG('path',{d:path.join(' '),fill:'none',stroke:'var(--yellow)','stroke-width':2}));
    // x ticks at 0, π/4, π/2, 3π/4, π
    [[0,'0'],[Math.PI/4,'π/4'],[Math.PI/2,'π/2'],[3*Math.PI/4,'3π/4'],[Math.PI,'π']].forEach(([t,lbl])=>{
      const x=ML+(W-ML-MR)*t/Math.PI;
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:x,y1:H-MB,x2:x,y2:H-MB+4,stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':0.8}));
      const tx=SVG('text',{x,y:H-MB+18,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':11,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      tx.textContent=lbl; svg.appendChild(tx);
    });
    // legend
    const lx=ML+12, ly=MT+8;
    svg.appendChild(SVG('rect',{x:lx-6,y:ly-4,width:175,height:48,fill:'var(--panel2)',stroke:'var(--line)','stroke-width':1,rx:4,opacity:0.92}));
    svg.appendChild(SVG('rect',{x:lx,y:ly+2,width:14,height:10,fill:'var(--green)'}));
    let t=SVG('text',{x:lx+20,y:ly+12,'font-size':11,fill:'var(--ink)'}); t.textContent='empirical histogram'; svg.appendChild(t);
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:lx,y1:ly+28,x2:lx+14,y2:ly+28,stroke:'var(--yellow)','stroke-width':2}));
    t=SVG('text',{x:lx+20,y:ly+32,'font-size':11,fill:'var(--ink)'}); t.textContent='(2/π)·sin²θ (USp)'; svg.appendChild(t);
    // readout
    out.textContent =
      'genus g = '+g+'    curves drawn: '+n+'    total angles binned: '+total+'\n'+
      (n>0
        ? 'as g grows, the green histogram tightens around (2/π)·sin²θ — Katz–Sarnak USp.'
        : '(click "draw 200 curves" to begin)');
  }
  function drawN(N){
    const g=+gSel.value;
    for(let c=0;c<N;c++){
      for(let i=0;i<2*g;i++){
        const t = sampleAngle(g);
        const k = Math.min(BINS-1, Math.floor(t/Math.PI*BINS));
        angles[g][k]++;
      }
      drawn[g]++;
    }
    render();
  }
  bDraw.addEventListener('click', ()=>drawN(200));
  bReset.addEventListener('click', ()=>{
    const g=+gSel.value; angles[g]=new Array(BINS).fill(0); drawn[g]=0; render();
  });
  gSel.addEventListener('change', render);
  render();
})();

6. Connections to $L$-functions and zeros

The Katz–Sarnak philosophy posits that every natural family of $L$-functions has a symmetry type — unitary $U$, orthogonal $O$, or symplectic $\mathrm{USp}$ — such that low-lying zeros (zeros near the central point $s=\tfrac12$) follow the eigenvalue statistics of the corresponding random-matrix ensemble. Empirically and conjecturally:

familysymmetry typedensity of $1$st zero near $\tfrac12$
$\zeta(s)$ alone$U$ (unitary)$1-\sin(\pi x)/(\pi x)$ (Montgomery)
$\{L(s,\chi_d)\}_{d}$ Dirichlet quadratic$\mathrm{USp}$ (symplectic)$1+\sin(2\pi x)/(2\pi x) - \cos(2\pi x)$
$\{L(s,E)\}_E$ elliptic-curve$O$ (orthogonal)repels at $x=0$
$\{L(s,f)\}_f$ holomorphic forms of fixed weight$O$ split by sign$O^+$ vs $O^-$ density

Why this matters arithmetically

Zero statistics encode arithmetic averages. For example, the $1$-level density of zeros of $L(s,\chi_d)$ near $s=\tfrac12$ predicts the proportion of $d$ for which $L(\tfrac12,\chi_d)\ne 0$ — a non-vanishing question equivalent to the BSD-on-average problem for quadratic twists. Soundararajan and Conrey–Soundararajan proved $\ge 87.5\%$ non-vanishing using moments + ratios, matching the Katz–Sarnak prediction.

Average-rank conjectures, the Iwaniec–Luo–Sarnak family-orthogonality results, and the Bhargava–Shankar Selmer averages all converge on the same picture: $L$-function families look like random-matrix ensembles, and which ensemble is dictated by the symmetry of the underlying motive.

<script>
(function(){
  const fSel=$('#sym-fam'), svg=$('#sym-svg'), out=$('#sym-out');
  const W=720, H=280, ML=60, MR=24, MT=28, MB=44;
  // 1-level density W(x) for each symmetry type (Katz–Sarnak).
  //   U:    1
  //   USp:  1 - sin(2πx)/(2πx)
  //   O+:   1 + sin(2πx)/(2πx)
  //   O-:   1 - sin(2πx)/(2πx) + δ_0   (the δ_0 we render as a tall spike at x=0)
  function W_of(fam, x){
    if(Math.abs(x)<1e-9) {
      if(fam==='U') return 1;
      if(fam==='USp') return 0;
      if(fam==='O+') return 2;
      if(fam==='O-') return 0;
    }
    const a = 2*Math.PI*x;
    const sinc = Math.sin(a)/a;
    if(fam==='U')  return 1;
    if(fam==='USp')return 1 - sinc;
    if(fam==='O+') return 1 + sinc;
    if(fam==='O-') return 1 - sinc;
    return 1;
  }
  function render(){
    const fam = fSel.value;
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    const xMin=0, xMax=3;
    const xpx=v=>ML+(W-ML-MR)*(v-xMin)/(xMax-xMin);
    const yMin=0, yMax=2.4;
    const ypx=v=>H-MB-(H-MT-MB)*(v-yMin)/(yMax-yMin);
    // grid
    for(let i=0;i<=6;i++){
      const yv=yMax*i/6, y=ypx(yv);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:ML,y1:y,x2:W-MR,y2:y,stroke:'var(--line)','stroke-width':0.5}));
      const t=SVG('text',{x:ML-8,y:y+4,'text-anchor':'end','font-size':11,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent=yv.toFixed(1); svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    [0,0.5,1,1.5,2,2.5,3].forEach(xv=>{
      const x=xpx(xv);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:x,y1:MT,x2:x,y2:H-MB,stroke:'var(--line)','stroke-width':0.4,'stroke-dasharray':'2 4'}));
      const t=SVG('text',{x,y:H-MB+18,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':11,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent=xv.toFixed(1); svg.appendChild(t);
    });
    // axis labels
    let t=SVG('text',{x:(ML+W-MR)/2,y:H-6,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':12,fill:'var(--mute)'});
    t.textContent='scaled height x'; svg.appendChild(t);
    t=SVG('text',{x:14,y:(MT+H-MB)/2,'font-size':12,fill:'var(--mute)','transform':`rotate(-90 14 ${(MT+H-MB)/2})`});
    t.textContent='W(x)'; svg.appendChild(t);
    // y=1 reference line
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:ML,y1:ypx(1),x2:W-MR,y2:ypx(1),stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':0.6,'stroke-dasharray':'4 6'}));
    // colour per family
    const COLS = {'U':'var(--cyan)','USp':'var(--violet)','O+':'var(--green)','O-':'var(--pink)'};
    const col = COLS[fam];
    // density curve
    const path=[];
    for(let i=0;i<=400;i++){
      const xv = xMin + (xMax-xMin)*i/400;
      // skip the very first sample for O- so the spike doesn't get connected
      if(fam==='O-' && i===0) continue;
      path.push((path.length?'L':'M')+xpx(xv).toFixed(2)+' '+ypx(W_of(fam,xv)).toFixed(2));
    }
    svg.appendChild(SVG('path',{d:path.join(' '),fill:'none',stroke:col,'stroke-width':2.5}));
    // O- delta at 0 — render as a tall arrow
    if(fam==='O-'){
      const x0=xpx(0), yT=ypx(yMax-0.1), yB=ypx(0);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:x0,y1:yB,x2:x0,y2:yT,stroke:col,'stroke-width':3.5}));
      svg.appendChild(SVG('polygon',{points:`${x0-6},${yT+4} ${x0+6},${yT+4} ${x0},${yT-6}`,fill:col}));
      const tt=SVG('text',{x:x0+10,y:yT+6,'font-size':12,fill:col,'font-style':'italic'});
      tt.textContent='δ₀'; svg.appendChild(tt);
    }
    // title: family description
    const desc = {
      'U':  'unitary U: W(x) = 1 (constant)',
      'USp':'symplectic USp: W(x) = 1 − sinc(2πx) — repulsion at x=0, density → 1',
      'O+': 'orthogonal O⁺: W(x) = 1 + sinc(2πx) — extra eigenvalue near x=0',
      'O-': 'orthogonal O⁻: W(x) = 1 − sinc(2πx) + δ₀ — forced zero spike',
    }[fam];
    t = SVG('text',{x:ML+12,y:MT-8,'font-size':12,fill:col,'font-weight':600});
    t.textContent = desc; svg.appendChild(t);
    // readout
    const samples=[0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0,1.5,2.0];
    let lines = 'family '+fam+'\n';
    lines += '  x      W(x)\n';
    samples.forEach(x=>{
      lines += '  '+x.toFixed(2)+'   '+W_of(fam,x).toFixed(4)+'\n';
    });
    out.textContent = lines;
  }
  fSel.addEventListener('change', render);
  render();
})();
</script>

blocks.html: Take-away. The bridge from arithmetic statistics to random matrices is not metaphor — it's a precise dictionary. Choose a family, identify its symmetry type, and the eigenvalue statistics of the matching random-matrix ensemble predict every reasonable family-average about the $L$-functions: zero locations, moments, non-vanishing proportions, $L'(\tfrac12)$ statistics, and (Bhargava–Shankar) the underlying Selmer / rank averages.

See also
  • Chebotarev density
  • Prototype L-functions

Used in
Random matrix theory · Katz–Sarnak symmetry of L-function families
</section>

Connections

Arithmetic statistics is open at every frontier: Malle's conjecture is wide open for $n\ge 6$, the Cohen–Lenstra heuristics for cubic and higher-degree fields are largely conjectural, the elliptic-curve average rank is conjecturally $\tfrac12$ but only proved $\le 1.17$ unconditionally, and the Katz–Sarnak symmetry assignment for high-rank automorphic families is in flux.

  • Algebraic number theory — class groups — the populations whose distribution Cohen–Lenstra describes.
  • Heights — Northcott finiteness — the height ordering is what makes "average" meaningful.
  • BSD — Bhargava–Skinner–Zhang prove BSD on average using Selmer averages.
  • $L$-functions and Sato–Tate — the random-matrix endpoint of the symmetry-type story.
  • Analytic number theory — moments of $\zeta$ and $L$-functions feed every density theorem.
